title: TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment
desc: Uses e-discovery to show defensible human–computer processes can save effort while oversight, relevance and stopping rules remain case-specific.

kps.k: E-discovery provides an early test of whether automation can reduce legal work without sacrificing defensible results.
kps.d: The sources frame technology-assisted review (TAR), especially machine-learning predictive coding, as a response to growing document volumes, expensive manual review and imperfect keyword retrieval. The substantive comparison is with fallible human processes, not perfect discovery. Automated Decision Support Technologies cites a 2012 RAND study of 57 cases in which review accounted for at least 70% of production costs in more than half the cases. This establishes an incentive to automate, not proof of savings from any particular system.

qs.q: CONCLUSION  [61] Overall, the myth that exhaustive manual review is the most effective – and therefore, the most defensible – approach to document review is strongly refuted.
qs.a: Technology-Assisted Review in E-Discovery Can Be More Effective and More Efficient Than Exhaustive Manual Review · Academia · 2011

kps.k: The strongest comparative evidence supports particular human–computer processes, especially on precision and review effort, rather than universal algorithmic superiority.
kps.d: Grossman and Cormack's 2011 analysis of TREC 2009 data found that selected H5 and Waterloo processes required humans to review an average 1.9% of documents. Precision and F1 gains were statistically significant at P < 0.001; the average recall difference was not significant at P > 0.1. They deliberately selected strong teams and inferred exhaustive-manual-review performance from sampled assessments rather than conducting a full-collection manual comparison. They report significance surviving a multiple-comparison correction, but the findings remain process-specific. Later judicial and scholarly citations to these results do not constitute independent replications, and reduced review effort does not directly measure total production savings.

qs.q: The technology-assisted reviews require, on average, human review of only 1.9% of the documents, a fifty-fold savings over exhaustive manual review.
qs.a: Technology-Assisted Review in E-Discovery Can Be More Effective and More Efficient Than Exhaustive Manual Review · Academia · 2011

kps.k: Judicial acceptance makes TAR available, but does not pre-approve every implementation or stopping decision.
kps.d: In Da Silva Moore, Judge Peck approved predictive coding based on the parties' agreement to use it, over three million documents, comparative suitability, proportionality and a transparent process; implementation remained disputed. He rejected perfection as the standard while requiring actual quality-control results before deciding when review could stop. Costs alone could not justify stopping, and consequential missed evidence could require retraining or further searches. Later accounts describe broader producing-party discretion, while the AI-Enhanced Lawyer reports that Victoria's practice note permits courts to order TAR in large cases without consent. These are context- and jurisdiction-specific developments, not blanket approval of GenAI.

kps.k: The principal governance disagreement concerns how much oversight preserves reliable disclosure without consuming TAR's savings.
kps.d: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice describes a shift from cooperation and methodological disclosure toward deference to producing parties, following concerns that negotiations and transparency requirements increased costs and discouraged adoption. Its authors also warn that lawyers can manipulate labels, model choices and validation to favor responding parties. Automated Decision Support Technologies adds interview evidence of confusion about recall, precision and reviewer effort, alongside some practitioners' belief in inherent algorithmic superiority. Its warning that selective checking could cause systematic under-disclosure is conditional, not a measured prevalence finding. Disclosure of training materials also raises confidentiality and privilege concerns.

kps.k: Automation reduces exhaustive review while retaining legal judgment, technical competence and responsibility for the process.
kps.d: Workflow accounts describe lawyers defining relevance, coding training material, correcting classifications and checking excluded documents. Continuous active learning repeatedly prioritizes documents for human review rather than eliminating human participation. Lawyers also select the review population, assess products and protocols, resolve uncertain classifications and defend the process. Can Robots Be Lawyers characterizes discovery's employment effect as strong, but supplies no numerical employment estimate and rejects complete displacement. Its upfront-cost qualification, and the AI-Enhanced Lawyer's 2019 large-litigation limitation, caution against treating historical economics as uniform across matters or current products. Opposing counsel also need enough statistical and technical understanding to assess production.

kps.k: GenAI's document-review results are promising but narrower than predictions that it will repeat TAR's adoption trajectory.
kps.d: Prompting Change compares Relativity's aiR for Review with human coding on 1,600 documents from one prior legal matter. It reports 83.9% recall and 84.7% precision for relevance, with variation by document type and more mixed issue coding. These findings do not establish superiority across matters, over earlier TAR methods, or on total cost. The authors call for broader empirical testing while predicting eventual normalization through a historical sequence of skepticism, validation and judicial acceptance. That analogy, like The Great Disruption's forecast of exponential improvement, remains a prediction rather than a demonstrated performance trend.

qs.q: For this case study, we worked with a client company and an eDiscovery vendor to select a 1,600-document sample from the client’s prior, real-life legal matter.

kps.k: The practical lesson advanced is to validate the complete review process, not rely on a technology label or transfer discovery results to all legal work.
kps.d: The sources emphasize product variation, training choices, sampling and task-specific performance. Recall measures relevant material retrieved; precision measures how much retrieved material is relevant. Reported agreements to 70% on each metric are practices, not universal legal standards, and aggregate scores do not settle the significance of omitted evidence. Evaluating Artificial Intelligence reports proposals for evidence-based tool selection and certification, not an established certification regime, and cautions that other legal tasks pose additional evaluation challenges. Predictions of higher provider profits or improved access to justice likewise require evidence beyond reductions in discovery effort; enterprise savings do not themselves demonstrate reduced unmet legal need.

vlens.an:
The selected academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition that TAR can sharply reduce exhaustive document review while retaining legal judgment, technical competence and responsibility. Their common reasoning is that discovery combines unusually large volumes and high manual-review costs with measurable retrieval tasks; however, the relevant comparator is fallible human review, and the strongest evidence concerns particular interactive human–computer processes rather than technology in the abstract.

This professional voice materially develops the proposition through empirical and governance contributions. Controlled studies quantify process-specific reductions in review effort and distinguish precision, recall and F1; workflow analyses locate lawyers’ continuing roles in defining relevance, training models, checking outputs, selecting protocols and defending review choices; and governance research calls for evidence-based validation while identifying risks from selective checking, manipulation and practitioner confusion over performance measures.

Material internal variation concerns evidential strength and governance emphasis. Some sources mainly forecast lower costs, wider adoption, provider profits or access-to-justice benefits, without demonstrating those downstream outcomes. Others supply controlled or case-specific evidence but stress limitations in study design, document type, matter size and transferability beyond e-discovery. The governance-oriented sources differ over how much transparency and oversight are desirable: disclosure and independent standards may improve defensibility, but burdensome negotiations or disclosure of training materials may erode savings or threaten privilege. Recent GenAI research extends the inquiry with promising results from one real matter while expressly calling for broader testing; its prediction of eventual normalization is more confident than its empirical base. These are positions within a curated selection and should not be treated as representative of academia generally.

qs.q: The particular processes found to be superior in this study are both interactive, employing a combination of computer and human input.
qs.a: Technology-Assisted Review in E-Discovery Can Be More Effective and More Efficient Than Exhaustive Manual Review · Academia · 2011

vlens.an: The supplied judicial source supports the proposition that technology-assisted review can reduce exhaustive document review while leaving legal judgment and responsibility with lawyers and courts. Da Silva Moore treats predictive coding as appropriate when justified by document volume, comparative suitability, cost-effectiveness, proportionality and process transparency—not as universally preferable or as a substitute for human judgment. Its central governance rationale is process-based: lawyers train the system, conduct quality control and remain responsible for relevance and production decisions, while courts assess the interaction between people and technology. The source also reinforces the proposition’s case-specific stopping rule: review should not end merely because automation promises savings; stopping depends on trained-system results that have been quality-control verified, considered alongside the stakes and significance of potentially missed evidence. Material qualification comes from the decision’s limited posture: the parties agreed to use predictive coding, disputed aspects of implementation, and the comparative performance claims were drawn from cited studies rather than measured outcomes in this litigation. Thus, this source offers conditional judicial acceptance rather than blanket approval of TAR, still less of GenAI or automation across legal work generally. Because only one judicial source is supplied for this professional voice, this finding characterises that source and should not be treated as representative of regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: The technology exists and should be used where appropriate, but it is not a ease of machine replacing humans: it is the process used and the interaction of man and machine that the courts needs to examine.
qs.a: Da Silva Moore v. Publicis Groupe & MSL Group, 287 F.R.D. 182 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 24, 2012) (Peck, M.J.) · Regulators & courts · 2012

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources support the proposition that technology-assisted review can sharply reduce exhaustive human document review while retaining legal judgment and requiring process-specific safeguards. Their common reasoning is that manual review is costly and fallible, whereas predictive coding can focus human effort through interactive human–computer workflows. The strongest empirical source reports substantial reductions in review effort and gains in precision and F1, but qualifies its conclusions because recall gains were not statistically significant, the comparison used selected high-performing teams, and the manual-review baseline was inferred. Da Silva Moore adds the principal governance foundation: TAR is appropriate only in suitable cases, and lawyers and courts must assess training, quality control, proportionality and verified stopping decisions rather than approve a technology label in the abstract. Internal variation is mainly evidentiary and predictive, not oppositional: Grossman and Cormack supply process-specific comparative evidence; Da Silva Moore translates that logic into conditional judicial acceptance; the quantitative-prediction source anticipates cost and profit effects without demonstrating them; and The Great Disruption extends the trajectory into more speculative forecasts of wider adoption and exponential improvement. These curated sources therefore support reduced review with retained responsibility, while differing over how much is demonstrated versus forecast and how fully governance requirements are specified.

elens.an: The curated 2015–2022 sources collectively support the proposition that technology-assisted review can substantially reduce exhaustive discovery work while leaving relevance judgments, validation, technology selection and stopping decisions with lawyers. Their common rationale is that escalating document volumes and review costs made manual review impractical, while keyword searches were both over- and under-inclusive; predictive coding offered a more scalable human–computer workflow measured against fallible human review rather than perfection. Material variation concerns economics and governance, not the core proposition. Some sources limit cost-effectiveness to large matters or note product- and dataset-specific weaknesses. Some principally describe efficiency, employment effects or conditional judicial acceptance and say relatively little about validation. Others materially strengthen the governance case by requiring statistical sampling, evidence-based tool and protocol selection, or proposed independent standards and certification. Practice-based work adds a sharper warning: controlled performance results do not establish how systems are used in practice, and selective, cost-driven checking could produce under-disclosure. The access-to-justice source extends expected efficiencies into a prospective social benefit, but does not demonstrate that reduced discovery effort has closed the justice gap. No supplied source rejects the proposition or advocates fully autonomous review.

elens.an: For the 2023–2024 “Generative shock” period, Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice supports the proposition that technology-assisted review can reduce document-review effort and cost without eliminating legal judgment. Its central reasoning is that TAR is a human–computer process: attorneys supply and revise relevance labels, while implementation quality, sampling, validation and stopping choices determine whether results are defensible. The source also supports case-specific governance rather than either blanket approval or maximal disclosure. Material internal variation concerns the appropriate degree of oversight: transparency can expose underperformance or strategic manipulation, but extensive negotiations and disclosure requirements may consume the savings that justify TAR. Its claims about comparative performance are qualified as contested and dependent on good implementation. The source principally addresses established TAR rather than providing direct evidence that generative AI will follow the same trajectory, so its support for the cluster’s GenAI-specific extension is indirect.

qs.q: Much of it stems from the fact that TAR, like            any machine learning system, is a socio-technical “assemblage,” not a turnkey            engine.26 Attorneys must label and re-label documents as the system works its way            toward a reliable model.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that AI-assisted document review and predictive coding can reduce review effort while improving relevance assessment. It describes tools that extract, organise and proofread document content, and presents predictive coding as more accurate than keyword searching. Its internal variation is principally cautionary rather than contradictory: it also notes costs and unresolved ethical questions, while its dramatic generative-AI productivity estimate is attributed to experts rather than demonstrated empirically. The source therefore aligns with the synthesis’s efficiency claim and general need for governance, but offers little concrete support for its more specific requirements concerning human verification, statistical validation, stopping rules and case-specific oversight. It supports rather than builds on the proposition because it does not materially develop those governance mechanisms. As a single curated source, it should not be treated as representative of legal-sector opinion or adoption generally.

The 2026 source accepts the proposition’s core lesson that automated document review should be judged as a defensible, task-specific process rather than assumed to be universally superior. It materially extends that lesson from established TAR to GenAI through a comparison with human coding on 1,600 documents from one real legal matter. The reported relevance results—83.9% recall and 84.7% precision—show promising potential to reduce review effort, while variation by document type, mixed issue-coding performance and identified tool limitations reinforce the continuing need for legal judgment, verification and matter-specific validation. The source also calls for testing across different matters and document sets, consistent with evaluating the complete workflow rather than relying on the GenAI label. Internal variation lies in its confidence: its empirical conclusions are cautious and case-specific, but its claim that GenAI adoption will be inevitable rests on a historical analogy to TAR and remains a prediction, not a demonstrated general trend. Because this period contains one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative or prevalent among 2026 sources generally.
